prerequisites: Elementary vector calculus. Concept of derivative and integral, with application to elementary functions.
System of linear equations and matrices.
Elementary concepts of particle kinematics and dynamics. Concept of force and Newton's principles. Work, kinetic and potential energy and conservation of energy.
Kinematics and dynamics of rigid body. Mass geometry. Moments of inertia.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences.
Ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Ability to work in a team.
Understanding and mastery of basic concepts on the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves, and electromagnetism and their application to solve problems typical of engineering.
Knowledge of the principles of machine and mechanism theory.
Analyze and kinematically synthesize mechanisms.
Pose and solve the direct and inverse dynamic problem of a planar mechanism.
Analyze and design rigid and flexible transmissions.
Know widely applied mechanisms and understand that many apparently very different mechanisms respond to the same kinematic principles.
Create kinematic diagrams of real mechanisms as a form of representation and understand the mechanism's operation from such a diagram.

Structurally analyze articulated mechanisms by criteria of nature and number of links or pairs, and by dimensional criteria, describing, as a consequence, the degrees of freedom or mobility of the mechanism and the existence or not of dead centers or return points and their singularities.
Know and develop the concepts, fundamentals, and methods applied to the kinematic and dynamic analysis of planar mechanisms.
Calculate velocities, accelerations, and forces in any planar mechanism, for specific positions of the mechanism and for complete cycles of motion.
Determine the type and dimensions of a bar mechanism to perform a specific function (problem known as mechanism synthesis).
Assimilate the relationships between actions and the movement they produce in machines and be able to recognize the type of dynamic problem associated with each case.
Determine the inertia effects supported by the links or bars that make up the mechanisms.
Correctly include friction forces in sliding, rotating pairs, and rolling and analyze and understand the operation of friction-based mechanisms.
Know and define the key dimensions and characteristics of motion transmissions between rotating shafts (gears, belts, ...).
Determine transmission ratios in ordinary and epicyclic gear trains and know the preferred design criteria used to define the number of teeth.
Describe the role played by cam mechanisms, highlighting their advantages and disadvantages in relation to other mechanisms that achieve the same results.
Use software for the analysis, simulation, and design of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and select information from various sources.
Develop the ability to understand and interpret the results obtained through kinematic and dynamic analysis of mechanisms and machines.

syllabus_topics: Mechanisms and machines. Basic concepts and schematization.
Definition, general structure and components of a machine
Classification of kinematic elements and pairs
Mobility of mechanisms: Grübler and Kutzbach criteria
Four-bar linkage and kinematic inversion. Grashof's law
Method of relative velocities and accelerations.
Direct dynamic analysis on reduced mechanisms
Flywheels: Steady state, degree of irregularity, concept of GD2
Sliding friction, in rotating pairs and rolling friction.
Concept of balancing. Balancing of mechanisms.
Fundamentals, terminology, and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Fundamentals, terminology, and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Ordinary and epicyclic trains. Willis's formula.
Fundamental design law and kinematics of cams.
teaching_methods: Laboratory / field / computer lab / language lab practices

assessment_methods.method: Continuous Assessment (EC): Problems done in classroom practices and/or tasks proposed by professors.
Laboratory practices (PL): Preparation, attitude, and submission of a report.
Final Exam (EF): Conceptual questions and problem-solving.

assessment_rules: For ordinary and extraordinary calls in June, if the minimum of 3 points out of 7.5 in the Final Exam is reached, the final grade is calculated as EC + PL + EF. If the minimum for the final exam is not reached, the course cannot be passed, and a grade of 4.9 will be recorded. For the extraordinary call in January and differentiated evaluation, a single written exam is required, covering the course topics (9 points) and laboratory practice content (1 point), with a minimum of 5 points out of 10 to pass. No programmable calculators or internet-enabled devices are allowed in exams. Grades from previous years are not carried over.
